nameStory: Red bistort gets its common name from its beautiful rose-red flower spikes and its twisted roots - 'bistort' comes from the Latin words meaning 'twice twisted.' The alternate name 'mountain fleece' refers to how its soft, downy flower spikes resemble woolly fleece, especially when they sway in mountain breezes.
description: Red bistort is a showy perennial flower that looks like it belongs in a fairy tale garden. This herbaceous plant grows up to 4 feet tall and wide, forming clumps of heart-shaped leaves topped with slender spikes of tiny rose-red or white flowers. Originally from the mountains of China and the Himalayas, it's occasionally found as a garden escape in New England, though it remains quite rare in our region.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Narrow, bottlebrush-like spikes of tiny rose-red or white flowers that feel soft and slightly fuzzy to the touch, blooming throughout summer

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves with pointed tips that feel smooth on top but noticeably downy and soft underneath - run your fingers along the underside

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense clumps up to 4 feet tall and wide, with multiple flower spikes rising above the leafy base like colorful candles

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Sturdy, upright stems that feel firm and substantial, often with a reddish tinge that complements the flower color

habitat: In New England, red bistort is extremely rare and typically found only as an occasional garden escape near old homesteads or abandoned cultivated areas. When it does establish, it prefers moist, rich soils in partial shade, similar to its native mountain habitat. Look for it in damp meadow edges or alongside streams where garden plants might have naturalized.

seasonality.spring: New heart-shaped leaves emerge and expand, feeling distinctly soft and downy on the undersides as the plant prepares for its summer show.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering season with prominent rose-red or white flower spikes that are unmistakable and bloom continuously through the warm months.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and leaves may develop autumn colors before the plant dies back to its root system for winter.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground roots, leaving no above-ground traces until spring returns.

funFact: Red bistort is so tough that it can survive at elevations over 14,000 feet in the Himalayas, making it one of the world's highest-altitude flowering plants - yet it's perfectly happy growing in a New England garden!
confusionNotes: The bottlebrush-like flower spikes might remind you of native smartweeds, but red bistort's heart-shaped leaves and much more robust size (up to 4 feet tall) easily distinguish it. Remember: heart-shaped leaves mean red bistort, narrow leaves mean smartweed.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'bistort,' this plant was recently moved from the genus Persicaria to Bistorta by botanists, so you might see it listed under either name in different field guides or websites. Garden centers often sell cultivars like 'Firetail' which may occasionally escape cultivation.
compareHints: Red bistort is much larger and more robust than its relatives alpine bistort and common bistort, both of which are smaller mountain plants. Red bistort's heart-shaped leaves and rose-red flower color also set it apart from common bistort's white flowers and alpine bistort's tiny stature and specialized high-altitude adaptations.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Alpine bistort is much smaller and more compact than its relatives common bistort and red bistort, which aren't found in New England.

Alpine bistort is much smaller and found only at high elevations with tiny bulblets replacing some flowers, while red bistort is a garden plant with much larger, more triangular leaves and showier red or pink flower spikes.
